english_translation: The wind blew strongly, and the trees swayed.

dialogue.english: The wind blew strongly, and the trees swayed.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Mhepo [wind / fresh air] • yakavhuvhuta [it (past) vhuvhuta] • nesimba [and / with simba] • miti [trees] • ikazununguka [ikazununguka]

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('yakavhuvhuta')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'yakavhuvhuta' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Joining Words with 'ne-' ('and / with') in 'nesimba'
grammar_notes.content: Look closely at 'nesimba'. In Shona, the word for 'and' or 'with' between nouns is not a separate word—instead, the prefix 'ne-' (or 'na-' before people's names) is written attached directly to the second noun! For example, 'ne-' + 'simba' forms 'nesimba'. You will see this everywhere in daily speech: 'sadza nemuriwo' ('sadza and vegetables'), 'nesimba' ('with strength'), and 'nekukasira' ('with haste / quickly').
grammar_notes.rule: ne- + Noun = and / with [Noun] (written as a single word, e.g., sadza nemuriwo = sadza and vegetables)

grammar_notes.title: How Shona Sentences Fit Together (Subject + Tense + Verb)
grammar_notes.content: In 'Mhepo yakavhuvhuta nesimba, miti ikazununguka.', notice how a single Shona verb word packs together who is doing the action (the subject prefix), when it happens (the tense marker), and the action itself (the verb stem). Once you recognize the building blocks at the start of the verb—like 'ndi-' (I), 'u-' (you), 'ti-' (we), or 'va-' (they)—you can immediately spot the subject even when no separate pronoun word is used!
grammar_notes.rule: [Who (Subject Prefix)] + [When (Tense Marker)] + [Action (Verb Root)] -> e.g., ti- (we) + -cha- (will) + -svika (arrive) = tichasvika

cultural_notes.title: August Winds ('Mhepo yaNyamavhuvhu') & Swaying Indigenous Trees
cultural_notes.content: The Shona name for the month of August is 'Nyamavhuvhu'—named directly after the verb '-vhuvhuta' ('to blow strongly'), because swirling winds sweep across the plateau in August, shaking the trees ('miti ikazununguka') and blowing away dry winter leaves.

active_exercises.prompt: How do you say 'Tall trees and green grass' in Shona?
active_exercises.explanation: 'Miti mirefu' = 'tall trees' (plural 'mi-' agreement on '-refu'), and 'neuswa hwegirinhi' = 'and green grass'.

active_exercises.prompt: In 'Shiri diki dziri kuimba pamusoro pemuti', what are the small birds doing?
options: Singing at the top of the tree
Looking for seeds in the field
active_exercises.correct_answer: Singing at the top of the tree
active_exercises.explanation: 'Shiri diki' = 'small birds', 'dziri kuimba' = 'are singing', 'pamusoro pemuti' = 'at the top of the tree'.

active_exercises.prompt: What does 'parutivi pemugwagwa' mean in 'Rori yakamira parutivi pemugwagwa'?
options: In the middle of the intersection
Beside the road / on the side of the road
active_exercises.correct_answer: Beside the road / on the side of the road
active_exercises.explanation: 'Parutivi pe-' means 'beside / at the side of', and 'mugwagwa' is 'road'.
